In E5, facing a genuinely unmeasurable crisis (his son in the NICU), he builds a feeding spreadsheet with a trend line and says explicitly 'there's no plan... But I needed my Google Sheet.' The mechanism is the same object recurring in three totally different stakes-levels — counting is not primarily about the domain (missionary work, sales, his son's health), it's a fixed way of converting helplessness into agency.
candidates.narrator_frame: He frames the counting as diligence or care ('I just wanted to know', 'I needed my Google Sheet') but never names it as a coping mechanism for lack of control.
candidates.form_evidence: The word-for-word repetition across decades — 'board,' 'masking tape,' 'spreadsheet,' 'trend line' — recurring in unrelated contexts (religion, sales, medicine) is itself the evidence; he never flags the pattern himself.

Each time he narrates the exit as chosen and values-driven, but the timing consistently precedes a moment where someone else's evaluation of him would become visible.

patterns.title: You turn helplessness into a spreadsheet, and the counting is the point, not the data.
patterns.description: From the masking-tape board on your apartment door in Brazil ("I made my own board. On the back of our apartment door with masking tape, a grid, every companionship in my district, every day, every number") to the Salesforce dashboard checked at 5:40am before Britt wakes, to the NICU feeding tracker you admit was unnecessary — "they had it all in Epic, they didn't need my Google Sheet. But I needed my Google Sheet" — this is the same move made in religious, professional, and medical contexts with nothing else in common. You never once frame it as a coping mechanism; each time you call it diligence or curiosity ("I just wanted to know"). Counterexample: the weekend you decided to leave the startup, you didn't build a tracker — you cleaned the garage for twelve hours instead, which suggests the real mechanism is broader than measurement: it's imposing order on anything uncontrollable, and counting is just your favorite version of that.
patterns.reasoning: This shows up in at least four separate life domains with near-identical language ("board," "masking tape," "spreadsheet," "trend line"). It would go up if you found a fifth instance outside sales/religion/health, and down if you could point to a high-stakes uncertain moment where you didn't build something to track it.
patterns.prediction: If you face a personal health scare (yours, not a dependent's), you'll start tracking a metric within days, independent of whether a doctor asked you to.

patterns.title: The truck rides with your silent father are the template, and you only named it once, at the very end, for one domain.
patterns.description: "That was, I'm not kidding, that was the closest I ever felt to my dad, was doing that" — ordering the day out loud, clipboard in hand — becomes the board, the dashboard, the sticky-note wall, the garage-organizing, and finally Council. You connect it yourself only in the last line of the last story: "My dad had the truck. I've got the doc. It's — I think it's the same thing, honestly." But you never make that connection for the board or the spreadsheet, where the same structure shows up without comment.
patterns.reasoning: Given the explicit throughline in your own words at the end. It would go up if Council or the boards ever came with real open-ended emotional conversation attached, not just an added "check-in section" — that would show the substitution isn't total.
patterns.prediction: As your kids get older and have real conflicts, you'll build a structured system (chore chart, meeting agenda) before or instead of having an unstructured conversation about it.

patterns.title: You say you believe in autonomy, then describe controlling your people more tightly than the manager you resented.
patterns.description: "I'm a big believer in autonomy. I really am" sits about twenty lines above "I'd take their deck and rebuild it and send it back at 11:40 pm and say 'just a couple tweaks!' with an exclamation point. Every time" — plus a private color-coded spreadsheet nobody asked for, and taking Kaylee's account from her before she could prove herself on it. You move from the claim to the contradicting stories without flagging the gap.
patterns.reasoning: The contradiction is internal to a single account and stated in your own words within one passage.
patterns.counterexample: You did genuinely refuse ride-alongs from your manager Doug for a full year, so the belief isn't empty — it's selective. You avoid being *watched*, but you practice invisible, artifact-based control over others.
patterns.prediction: In your current nine-person company, you'll still personally review or redo team output rather than fully delegate, even while describing yourself as hands-off.

patterns.title: You forgo clear money for autonomy, and you can name the exact price.
patterns.description: You turned down seed funding over a board seat and said so plainly: "We'd probably be at four or five million right now if I'd taken it. Like, probably. My buddy Sam took money and he's at eleven. Eleven! But I sleep. That's the trade." That's not vague regret — it's a costed decision, stated once, without hedging.
patterns.reasoning: It would weaken if you pursued additional funding rounds without hesitation in years three to five.
patterns.counterexample: Taking Kaylee's account from her suggests the real driver might be narrower than "ownership" broadly — it may specifically be discomfort with being answerable to someone *above* you, not a general principle about control.
patterns.prediction: You'll resist bringing on a co-founder-level partner or equity investor in the future, even when it would clearly speed growth, and you'll cite autonomy, not risk, as the reason.

patterns.title: You leave or cede ground right before someone else's judgment of you would become visible, then explain the exit as chosen for other reasons.
patterns.description: You quit wrestling the night before the wrestle-off ("And I quit on the Monday"), sent your letter asking not to be promoted on the mission two weeks before transfer calls, and gave notice at the startup three weeks before a reorg you suspected would pass you over anyway: "I probably would've been in the mix. Maybe... It probably would've gone to Priya." Each time you frame the exit as driven by something else — money, calling, product vision — and defend the sincerity of that ("And I meant it!"). But you also volunteer the precise timing that undercuts the frame, unprompted, every time.
patterns.reasoning: The pattern holds three times but the underlying motive (avoidance vs. genuine principle) is inferred, not stated by you. It would go up with a fourth clean instance, down if you'd ever stayed through to the outcome and only left after an unfavorable result.
patterns.counterexample: With Kaylee's account, you did the opposite — you seized ground rather than ceded it, taking the account before she could prove herself on it. So this isn't general evaluation-avoidance; it looks more like you pre-empt exposure to being judged yourself while staying comfortable judging others' readiness.
patterns.prediction: When a major decision is pending that could reveal whether your approach was wrong, you'll make a unilateral change before the decision point rather than after.

patterns.title: Relief, for you, shows up physically only when you're NOT chosen — not when you are.
patterns.description: "I felt so relaxed. Like my shoulders came down. Physically" describes being passed over for zone leader — a moment you mislabeled at the time as "the Spirit confirming it." Avoiding the Park City leadership offsite gets the same treatment: "honestly a weekend in Park City doing trust falls with Marcus? No thank you. I would've found a way out of it." Nowhere in what you've told me is there an equivalent physical description of relief or joy at being selected or promoted.
patterns.reasoning: It would firm up with a clear instance of genuine disappointment at being passed over somewhere in your history — that's currently missing.
patterns.counterexample: Your four promotions at the startup were pursued and seemingly enjoyed, with no relief described at any point you were passed over there — so this isn't a blanket aversion to advancement, it's specific to visibility under a powerful individual evaluator (mission president, Marcus) versus reward tied to output (a leaderboard).
patterns.prediction: If offered a board seat, advisory title, or public leadership role, you'll hesitate or decline more often than not, citing time or values reasons that sit on top of relief at avoiding visibility.

patterns.title: Pride in an achievement gets deflated by you within the very next sentence — but only in adult, professional contexts.
patterns.description: After describing being "obsessed" with the board and #1 for nine weeks on the mission, you immediately go to reading the fax alone in the bathroom "because it felt weird to be that happy about it in front of everybody." After listing four promotions in five years, you immediately add: "Which sounds great and honestly a lot of it was just that the company was doubling."
patterns.reasoning: Three instances with one clean counterexample. It would strengthen with a fourth adult achievement described without hedging turning up as evidence against the pattern, or weaken if one showed no deflection at all.
patterns.counterexample: Your wrestling record gets no such treatment — you state it with pride and double down at the very end ("I still think I would've beat Tanner"), no deflation attached. That's a clean break: the reflex shows up specifically once you're in professional or adult territory, not in the adolescent story.
patterns.prediction: When asked directly what you're most proud of building, you'll name the team or circumstances before naming your own contribution, even when asked specifically for your part.

patterns.title: The Everton relationship outlived the story — it's not just a good anecdote, it's still running.
patterns.description: "He sends me a message every single New Year's. Every year" is evidence independent of anything you're telling an interviewer — it's ongoing, unprompted from the other side. Combined with choosing the low-status posting at Ivaiporã and eating dinner with the same family "like forty times," this points to durable investment beyond a polished story. You're also honest about the ambiguity in your own motives there — you don't fully resolve whether Ivaiporã was service or self-protection, which is notable restraint.
patterns.reasoning: It would go up with evidence of a second multi-decade relationship you still actively maintain, not just remember fondly.
patterns.counterexample: The same story shows the promotion-avoidance may have been partly self-protective, which tempers but doesn't erase the independently-verified relationship.
patterns.prediction: You have at least one other multi-decade friendship from an earlier chapter of your life that you're still in active contact with.

patterns.title: When you miss someone emotionally, you repair it with logistics in a different, more controllable register — not with the thing that was actually asked for.
patterns.description: You let Britt's call go once during the placental emergency and still carry it: "I still think about the fact that I let it go the first time." What follows is an escalation of adjacent service — coffee runs, Costco trays, sitting by the isolette with printouts — rather than direct repair. When Britt asked you plainly to "just sit down," you lasted six minutes: "And I lasted, I'm not exaggerating, maybe six minutes. And then I went and got coffee for the nurses."
patterns.reasoning: Mostly grounded in this one account, with the six-minutes-then-coffee moment as the clearest real-time instance. It would strengthen with a second instance elsewhere in your life of the same substitution.
patterns.counterexample: Council, which came out of this same period, became a genuine and sustained relational structure Britt experiences as "the best thing in our marriage" — so this isn't purely evasive; you did eventually build something that connects, even if it's still shaped like a doc.
patterns.prediction: When you miss or fail at an emotionally significant moment with your kids as they get older, you'll respond with more logistical or provider effort rather than a direct repair conversation.
